Title: Why I Stopped Chasing the Perfect Tech Stack
Content: Every six months a new framework promises to solve everything. I've been building software for eight years and I've seen this cycle repeat: excitement, adoption, disillusionment, replacement. The engineers who thrive long-term are not the ones who chase the newest thing — they're the ones who deeply understand tradeoffs. React vs Vue doesn't matter. SQL vs NoSQL doesn't matter. What matters is whether you can articulate why you chose something and what you gave up to get it. My current stack: FastAPI, PostgreSQL, React, deployed on Google Cloud Run. It's boring. It works. I can hire people who know it. I can debug it at 2am. That's the real evaluation criteria.

Title: Building AI Products That Actually Stick
Content: Most AI features get deprecated within a year. The ones that survive share a common trait: they save users from a task they genuinely hated doing, not a task that seemed impressive to demonstrate. I've shipped four AI features in the last two years. Two are still alive. The two that survived are unglamorous: an email categorizer and a document summarizer. Nobody demos them. Everyone uses them daily. The graveyard is full of chatbots that could do everything and solved nothing in particular. When building AI products, start with the most specific problem. Solve it completely. Then expand. The biggest mistake is starting broad.

Title: The Case for Radical Async Communication
Content: Our team spent 2023 eliminating synchronous communication wherever it wasn't strictly necessary. The results surprised us. Meeting hours dropped by 60%. Written communication quality improved dramatically — people think more carefully when they can't rely on real-time clarification. Onboarding new engineers became easier because everything was documented. The tradeoff: it requires more upfront work to communicate clearly. A five-minute meeting becomes a ten-minute written brief. But that brief is searchable, referenceable, and doesn't interrupt anyone's flow state. For knowledge work, async-first is not a compromise. It's an upgrade. The synchronous meeting should be the exception reserved for genuine ambiguity and relationship building — not status updates and decision reviews.

Title: What Vector Databases Actually Changed
Content: Before vector databases went mainstream, semantic search required either expensive embedding infrastructure or accepting keyword-based limitations. The shift changed how we think about knowledge retrieval entirely. Instead of asking 'does this document contain these words', we now ask 'is this document conceptually similar to this query'. The implications are substantial. Support ticket classification that used to require hundreds of labeled examples now works with a dozen. Document search that used to miss synonyms now finds conceptually related content. The technology is not magic — the quality of your embeddings and chunking strategy determines everything. But the fundamental capability shift is real and permanent. We are early in understanding the full design space of retrieval-augmented systems.
